2024 · EMNLP 2024 · Benchmarks & Evals

AssistantBench: Can Web Agents Solve Realistic and Time-Consuming Tasks?

214 hand-collected, automatically-verifiable web tasks that take a person several minutes of open-web browsing to answer — real-estate monitoring, business hours, tuition fees — plus SPA, a planning-and-memory upgrade to SeeAct. No system tops 26.4 accuracy points on the test set, and the paper's SOTA web-agent baseline, SeeAct alone, scores 4.1 (GPT-4-Turbo) to 2.2 (Claude-3.5-Sonnet).

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By mid-2024, benchmarks for LLM-based web agents mostly asked models to complete a task inside a single site or a static sandbox: MiniWoB++ (Liu et al., 2018) simulates form-filling widgets, WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) is scoped to one shopping site, Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023) and WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) evaluate action sequences within a fixed set of sandboxed websites. These benchmarks were essential for building better agents, but they don't test whether an agent can plan and reason across the open web the way a person actually does when, say, checking which nearby gyms have an early class or tracking a local real-estate listing. The closest prior benchmark, GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024), does test open-web assistant tasks, but many of its questions also require video or audio tools — even the 90-task web-only subset used by WebVoyager (He et al., 2024) includes a question about counting bird species in a YouTube video — which conflates web navigation skill with multi-modal tool use.

AssistantBench targets a narrower, cleaner slice: tasks that are (1) realistic — a real information need a person had, (2) time-consuming — at least several minutes of manual browsing, and (3) automatically verifiable — a closed-form answer that won't drift with time. The authors argue no existing benchmark isolates open-web navigation and reasoning this cleanly while staying answerable without video/audio tooling, and set out to measure just how far current closed-book, retrieval-augmented, and agentic systems are from being useful there.

// how it works

The method

AssistantBench's 214 tasks were built in three stages. First, 18 people the authors had direct contact with (colleagues, friends) shared time-consuming web-browsing tasks they had recently done themselves, each manually reviewed and, when necessary, tweaked (e.g., adding a date constraint) to keep the answer stable over time. Second, crowd-workers were shown a seed task as a template — e.g., "What Daniel Craig movie under 150 minutes and on Netflix US has the highest IMDB rating?" — and asked to write structurally similar tasks of their own, expanding the general set. Third, 35 domain-expert crowd-workers recruited on Prolific (fluent English, ≥99% approval rate, ≥50 prior submissions) shared realistic tasks from their own professional fields — biology, law, medicine, geography, visual arts among them — after a qualification round that filtered out websites requiring logins or with too little interaction. The final tally, per the paper's data-statistics section: 214 unique tasks — 172 from the general seed-and-expansion pipeline and 42 from the expert set — whose gold answers are spread across more than 525 webpages on 258 different websites. A held-out 33-task development set (12 seed, 21 crowd-expanded) supports prompt iteration separately from the test set.

Because tasks have open-ended natural-language answers, the paper defines a per-type scoring function rather than plain exact match. String answers are scored with word-level F1 against the gold string; list answers use the alignment-based scorer from DROP (Dua et al., 2019); numeric answers get partial credit that decays with how many orders of magnitude the prediction is off, floored at zero once it's off by a full order of magnitude:

score = max { 0,  1 − log max(A, A′)min(A, A′) } // A = gold number, A′ = predicted number; used for numeric answers only

Some tasks call for structured dict answers (e.g., a JSON mapping each daycare center to its tuition); these are scored by matching values for identical keys and averaging recall (over gold keys) and precision (over predicted keys) into an F1, using the string or numeric scorer per value type. Beyond this per-task accuracy, the paper also reports answer rate (the fraction of tasks the model didn't abstain on), precision (accuracy restricted to answered tasks), and strict exact match (1 only if the prediction equals the gold string verbatim, 0 otherwise) — a deliberate four-way breakdown because, as the results show, accuracy alone conflates "answers confidently and is usually right" with "answers almost everything and is right often enough to add up."

On the agent side, the paper's new baseline is SPA (See-Plan-Act), built directly on top of SeeAct (Zheng et al., 2024). SeeAct's per-step loop is: take a screenshot, describe in natural language what the next action should be, then ground that description onto a specific HTML element to click, type into, or otherwise act on. SPA keeps that grounding step but wraps it with two additions: a planning component that lets the model write and revise a running plan at each step, and a memory buffer the model can write task-relevant facts into and carry across steps — both implemented purely through prompting, with no additional training. SPA is also given new web-navigation actions SeeAct lacked: go back to the previous page, jump directly to a URL, and issue a query to a search engine. Both agents are capped at 30 execution steps, following prior evidence that agents tend to succeed quickly and fail slowly.

// what they found

The results

The paper evaluates six model configurations against the AssistantBench test set, each with both a GPT-4-Turbo and a Claude-3.5-Sonnet backbone: two closed-book LMs prompted with chain-of-thought (zero-shot CB-INST, and one-shot self-ask CB-1S), two retrieval-augmented LMs that call Google Search via SerpAPI (zero-shot RALM-INST, one-shot RALM-1S), the existing web agent SeeAct, and the paper's own SPA — plus four ensembles that fall back to CB-1S whenever an agent/RALM abstains. Table 1 below reproduces the GPT-4-Turbo results on the test set exactly as the paper reports them; none of the ten rows is comparable to any other benchmark's numbers, and none should be read across the GPT-4-Turbo/Claude-3.5-Sonnet split.

Configuration (GPT-4-Turbo, test set)Acc.Ans. %Prec.EM
CB-INST (closed-book, zero-shot)16.553.630.76.1
CB-1S (closed-book, one-shot)22.289.524.88.3
RALM-INST (retrieval, zero-shot)11.860.219.55.5
RALM-1S (retrieval, one-shot)10.748.122.43.9
SeeAct (web agent)4.115.526.32.2
SPA (web agent, ours)11.135.930.95.5
RALM-INST→CB (ensemble)18.793.919.96.6
RALM-1S→CB (ensemble)19.592.821.06.1
SeeAct→CB (ensemble)23.489.526.19.4
SPA→CB (ensemble, ours)25.291.727.59.9

With GPT-4-Turbo, no configuration in Table 1 tops 25.2 accuracy — that ceiling belongs to the SPA→CB ensemble. SPA alone reaches 11.1 accuracy against SeeAct's 4.1: about 7 accuracy points higher, with roughly 2.3× the answer rate (35.9% vs. 15.5%) and 4.6 precision points higher (30.9 vs. 26.3). Closed-book CB-1S actually posts higher raw accuracy (22.2) than either agent, but almost entirely on volume — it answers 89.5% of tasks at only 24.8 precision, i.e., it is wrong on roughly three-quarters of the tasks it answers. With Claude-3.5-Sonnet as the backbone (Appendix Table 7), the same pattern holds: SeeAct alone scores 2.2 accuracy, SPA alone reaches 12.9, and the SPA→CB ensemble reaches 26.4 accuracy with 13.8 exact match — the single highest accuracy and exact-match figure the paper reports on the AssistantBench test set across either backbone. That 26.4 is also the number behind the paper's own framing that "no model reaches an accuracy of more than 26 points" on AssistantBench.

On FanOutQA (Zhu et al., 2024) — a Wikipedia-only multi-hop QA set the authors repurpose as a second dev-style check, restricted to 31 dictionary-answer questions that GPT-4-Turbo's CB-1S doesn't already answer perfectly — the same GPT-4-Turbo SPA reaches 30.0 accuracy at 61.3% answer rate and 48.9 precision, versus SeeAct's 7.5 accuracy at 16.1% answer rate and 46.4 precision: a 22.5-point accuracy gap and roughly 45 percentage points higher answer rate, with SPA also reaching the literal reference answer (exact match 9.7) on 3 of 31 tasks, more than any other system there.

Manual error analysis (on the 33-task dev set) attributes most SPA and SeeAct failures to not producing an answer at all (80% of SPA's errors, 97% of SeeAct's), broken down as navigation errors (36.7% of SPA errors, 63.6% of SeeAct's — the single largest cause for both), grounding failures (23.3% / 18.2%), technical crashes (16.7% / 9.1%), and "saw the right answer but didn't return it" (3.3% / 6.1%); wrong-answer errors, by contrast, make up 20.0% of SPA's errors but only 3.0% of SeeAct's, i.e., SPA's stronger answer rate buys more coverage at some cost in wrong answers. Closed-book errors are dominated by hallucination (85%) over outdated facts (15%); retrieval-augmented errors are dominated by failure to retrieve relevant information (80%), split further into tool-shaped needs the retriever can't serve (38.5%), partial retrieval (11.5%), and irrelevant context (50%).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The headline "no model tops 26 points" framing is honest as stated, but it aggregates across four structurally different mechanisms — closed-book guessing, retrieval, agentic web navigation, and ensembles of the two — whose accuracy numbers are driven by different things and shouldn't be read as a single leaderboard. CB-1S's 22.2 accuracy (GPT-4-Turbo, test set) comes from answering 89.5% of tasks at a precision of only 24.8: it is a model that almost never says "I don't know" and is wrong most of the time it does answer, not a model that reliably knows things. SeeAct's 4.1 accuracy comes from the opposite failure mode — it abstains on 84.5% of tasks (15.5% answer rate) but is relatively precise (26.3) on the few it attempts. Collapsing both into one "accuracy" column, as Table 1 does, makes CB-1S look 18.1 points stronger than SeeAct (22.2 vs. 4.1) — but the more informative comparison, precision-vs-precision, actually flips the ranking: SeeAct's 26.3 precision beats CB-1S's 24.8, despite SeeAct scoring far lower on the headline metric purely because it answers so much less often. The paper's own inclusion of answer-rate and precision columns is exactly the right move here, but the abstract's single "26 points" headline doesn't carry that nuance forward.

The ensemble numbers deserve similar care: SPA→CB's 25.2 (GPT-4-Turbo) or 26.4 (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, the paper's single highest reported figure on the test set) is not "SPA solving more of the benchmark" — it's SPA navigating the web when it can (35.9% / 34.3% answer rate) and falling back to a closed-book guess the rest of the time. Given CB-1S alone already reaches 22.2 (GPT-4-Turbo) or 21.9 (Claude) accuracy on this same benchmark, most of an ensemble's headline number is attributable to the closed-book fallback, not to the agent's own web navigation — a point the paper's design makes transparent (it names them "ensembles," reports SPA's un-ensembled 11.1/12.9 alongside), but which a reader skimming only the abstract's "26 points" could miss entirely.

On error analysis: the 36.7%/63.6%-style navigation-error breakdowns (Table 4) and the retrieval-failure breakdown (tool-shaped 38.5%, partial 11.5%, irrelevant 50%) are computed over the 33-task development set, not the 214-task test set — with that few tasks and a nontrivial fraction abstaining or erroring, a single dev-set example is worth roughly 3 percentage points in Table 4 (denominators of 30 for SPA and 33 for SeeAct), so the precise splits should be read as illustrative rather than statistically stable. The paper doesn't report confidence intervals or repeated-run variance for any of its point estimates (the step-count plots — Figure 5, plus appendix Figs. 12–13 — are the only place error bars appear, and even there each bin holds relatively few tasks). A separate, informal check on ChatGPT with web search and code execution (again on the dev set) found it erring on more than 90% of tasks, with the dominant failure mode being over-reliance on a search result to produce a confidently wrong answer, plus a smaller pattern (~15% of cases) of hallucinating data inside the code interpreter that the user never sees generated — this isn't one of the paper's scored configurations, but it's the most externally-legible evidence in the paper that the gap generalizes past the specific models benchmarked.

baselines

Fair for their moment (GPT-4-Turbo / Claude-3.5-Sonnet-era) but narrow: every configuration is built on exactly two closed proprietary backbones (the paper's own Limitations section flags this — open-weight Llama-3.2 experiments are described as "in-progress" and never land in the paper), and the single web-agent baseline is SeeAct, reused with two tweaks (US locale, 30-step cap) rather than benchmarked against other open-web agents at the time (e.g., WebVoyager). There is no comparison to a human upper bound on the test set itself.

contamination

Tasks are freshly authored by contacted participants and crowd-workers rather than scraped from an existing corpus, which limits classic train-test contamination. But the paper is candid that some answers can drift with time; its own §6.4 splits tasks into static (43.5%), stable-but-changeable (15.4%), and longer-horizon-changeable (41.1%) categories and shows accuracy stays under 21 points on the static+stable splits for every GPT-4-Turbo configuration — reassuring for near-term reuse, but the benchmark carries no mechanism (e.g., a rolling/held-out leaderboard split) to stop future model pretraining corpora from absorbing its now-public gold answers and explanations.

what's missed

The single "accuracy" number hides the precision/answer-rate tradeoff described above, and hides that the highest reported figures (25.2 / 26.4) are ensemble numbers substantially carried by a closed-book fallback rather than by successful agentic browsing. Per-example cost is also absent from the headline results: Appendix Table 6 shows SeeAct and SPA cost roughly $2.09–$2.47 per example to evaluate versus $0.006–$0.07 for the closed-book/retrieval models — a 30–400× cost gap for a single-digit-to-low-teens accuracy gain that the main results tables don't surface.

would raise confidence

Open-weight agent baselines actually completed (not just flagged as in-progress); a larger, independently-sampled error-analysis set instead of the 33-task dev set so the Table 4 percentages carry real statistical weight; repeated runs with variance reported for the headline accuracy numbers, since single-run web-navigation results are known to be noisy; and separating "agent-only" from "ensemble-with-fallback" numbers in the abstract/headline rather than only in the appendix tables.

// bottom line

AssistantBench is a genuinely useful, carefully-constructed stress test — 214 tasks that took real people minutes to solve manually expose real gaps between "sounds confident" and "actually right." But its headline "26 points" number is an ensemble ceiling built from a closed-book fallback plus an agent that alone reaches only 11–13 accuracy points, on a proprietary two-backbone baseline set, evaluated for error analysis on just 33 tasks — read the paper's own per-configuration table before repeating the top-line number.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AssistantBench tests open-web, multi-site navigation on 214 realistic, time-consuming tasks, deliberately outside the single-site/sandbox scope of MiniWoB++, WebShop, Mind2Web, and WebArena, and outside GAIA's video/audio-tool tasks — collected from 18 seed contributors, crowd-worker expansion, and 35 domain experts, spread across 525 webpages and 258 sites.
  2. On the test set, no configuration the paper reports tops 26.4 accuracy (SPA→CB, Claude-3.5-Sonnet backbone) — but that ceiling is an ensemble number carried substantially by a closed-book fallback; the paper's own new agent, SPA, reaches only 11.1 (GPT-4-Turbo) to 12.9 (Claude) accuracy on its own, versus SeeAct's 4.1 / 2.2.
  3. Closed-book models look competitive on raw accuracy only because they rarely abstain — on the AssistantBench test set, CB-1S answers 89.5% of tasks at only 24.8 precision (and on FanOutQA, CB-1S's answer rate reaches 100%) — a gap the paper's four-metric reporting (accuracy, answer rate, precision, exact match) surfaces but the "26 points" headline does not.
